utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Tuesday, 9th of October. I would like to welcome all those present, Mr. Scott, the counsels, the accused, as well as all those present in the courtroom. Mr. Scott wanted to take the floor, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone in the courtroom. Very briefly, just again, because I know we tend to get very busy in the course of the day, I didn't want to forget it again until later today. It's simply to request the opportunity to respond to a couple of Defence filings, Your Honour, in connection with the testimony of Dr. Miller, and I had indicated that this doesn't need to be -- none of this really needs to be in closed session or outside of the hearing of the witness. In connection with the evidence given by Dr. Miller, the -- I believe it's the Praljak Defence and the Petkovic Defence have filed oppositions to certain documents, and the Prosecution would like to have -- ask the Chamber's leave to have until Friday to file a response concerning that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall entertain this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Scott, you've used up three hours almost, two hours and 54 minutes, so you have almost three hours, which means you have another hour. Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. I was going to raise this matter in the absence of the witness, but perhaps I can raise it now. It's an application for Your Honours to vary, if you're minded, the order yesterday that a response be filed by the Defence in writing in relation to an application of the Prosecution by Thursday. Your Honour will recollect the order made yesterday morning. Your Honour, I wonder, given that we have another deadline to file on Thursday, if Your Honours would be minded to give the Defence ten or 15 minutes today or tomorrow just to respond orally. It is a very discrete issue, and it would alleviate some of the of the burden of actually putting something down in writing. Of course, the transcript and the oral submissions would, I think, be enough to guide Your Honours on the issue as far as the Defence submissions are concerned, and I think it's a matter that the Prosecution could respond to summarily in any event. Your Honour, it would ease the burden on the Defence, and it is my application that Your Honours grant ten minutes tomorrow or today to respond orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What we'll do is we'll start with this one and a half hour session, then when we resume later on. Before the witness is called in, you will have ten minutes to make your point. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly in response to Mr. Scott's request. We didn't -- we did not file anything because we have extensively put our position on the record, and we would just invite the Prosecution to take those comments in mind as well, when they do respond, that they probably should respond to -- to our comments and our objections on the record. We certainly don't want to give the impression that we waived any interest in -- in our objections to Mr. Miller's testimony. They are on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rupcic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to continue on with a few additional examples of these banking transactions. We finished yesterday one concerning a transfer from something called the "DSK" involving Mr. Stojic. I'd like to ask you to turn now to a bundle, sort of a collection of various transactions, that have collectively been marked as P 10297. These transactions are organised in a chronological way. So what I'll be doing, because we won't have time to go through every single transaction, of course, what I'd like to do is point you to several of them. I will do it chronologically, so we'll all just need to be able to turn through the document to the date order approximately. The First document is dated 29th of January, 1993, and I believe the last document in the bundle is dated the 12th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sure you understand, given the time limitations, we have not tried to present or go through every single document of this nature. That would take some days, if not weeks, to go through every single transaction record that we have in these matters. So we can give the Chamber an overview of the types of records that were being kept at this time and a sampling of some of the transactions that are reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this bundle, Mr. Rupcic, I'd like to turn your attention, if you could go, to the -- there is a card, one of these public auditing service cards that we looked at yesterday, reflecting a transaction on the 17th of February 1993. So if you can please turn into the document until you get to the transaction for the 17th of February involving a transaction of 454 -- excuse me, 454.658.000 dinars. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just simply wanted to, again, review a couple of things we talked about yesterday. Is it correct, then, again on this particular card, you can say that it was a telephone or telegraph transaction or approval, which meant that this transaction could essentially be taken -- take place immediately? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you -- if you can recall the accounts that we looked at yesterday, I direct your attention to the account number which is immediately above on the right side of the form, immediately above the date and the place Metkovic. In the box above that, again we have the number 80822 and following. Can you just simply confirm that is the account number for what we would call the "HVO Grude" or "HVO military account"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the left side, the purpose of the transfer is indicated as "Payment of special disbursement from the Ministry of Defence." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could next ask you to turn through the bundle until you get to a transaction, please, there maybe two on this date, so we'll have to be sure we're referring to the same one. On the 16th, the first transaction indicated for the 16th of April, 1993. This is a transaction for 500.000.000 Croatian dinars on the 16th of April. Again, I'll just ask you to, if you can confirm for us once again, the signatures on the requests for cash withdrawal, who authorised that withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic and Mr. Bandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that -- I think we're looking at a different transaction.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The transaction on the 16th of April for 500.000.000. Can you tell us, if you've found that, can you please tell us who signed the authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelavic and Mr. Majic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Go ahead. I thought I interrupted you. Did you have something else to say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jelavic and Mr. Majic signed this. Is this the 16th of April? Is that the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you. Thank you, sir. Can you confirm on the document, the other document that's related to this, that that does bear your signature as the person who received the funds?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we also just confirm, when we look at this transaction, this money was withdrawn from again what we call the "HVO Mostar" or "finance department" account?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If you remember, when we talked, I told you that the two of them could not have been signatories on this account, so that is an admission on the part of the bank; the fact that it was allowed, that is to say, this cash withdrawal, given these signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to be clear on what you're indicating, Mr. Jelavic and Mr. Majic were signatories on the HVO Grude or military account but not on this particular account; nonetheless, you confirm the transaction did take place and you were the one that actually collected the 500.000.000 dinars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could next ask you to go to, toward the end of the document, the first of the documents that are dated - because, again, there are two on this date - but the first document dated the 12th of November, 1993. By way of reference, I'll refer to the dinar amount, 12.447.600 dinar on the 12th of November, 1993. This, again, refers to being taken from the DSK, and this is indicated as coming from the -- from a Grude account. Can you look at the documents and tell us -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the account in Grude but from the savings account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, from one of the savings currency account, the foreign currency savings accounts that you mentioned yesterday; correct? In this particular instance, do you agree that, although it's fairly faint --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. We were talk over each other. Do you agree that you signed for this cash as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the rubric that says "Purpose," you will see my name and surname and the number of my ID. I collected the money. It is 3.280 deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall on this occasion or is there anything on this particular document that indicates whether you actually withdrew that cash in either the dinar or deutschmark?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it's obvious, since there is no specification, that it's dinars. Since it involved an enormous number of banknotes, they could not provide a specification. If it had been in deutschmark, they would have given a specification as to if it was 100, 500, or 1.000 deutschmark bills.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We just have a couple more of these to go. Now, back in the main binder or continuing in the main binder, if you could go to P 01934. If you have that, sir, can you confirm that this is a transaction on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This appears to be drawn on an account for the finance department in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- actually, I apologise. It is correct. This is an order regarding a transfer from the Mostar account to the account of the HVO, the military section of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of those persons who authorised the transaction, once again, if you can turn to that particular page, can you identify, please, for us the signatures of the persons who authorised this transfer from the finance department to the HVO military account?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got that document. Here you cannot see who approved this, which persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you may have gone to the --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document afterwards is the request for cash withdrawal, and it's from the military account. If you look at the number, it is the military section; that is to say, once the money was transferred to the military part, then the request for cash withdrawal was related to the military part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who signed the request for cash withdrawal then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bruno Stojic and Mr. Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic's signature being the one on the line on the left side of the line and Mr. Jelavic's signature being the one on the right side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honours, but on the first page of the document under the same number on this document, "Sale," it says, in handwritten, "Wrong order. Stopped." So, according to this document, this document was not carried through. Perhaps the witness could explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's correct. If you can see here, it says here, "Payment of cash from non-resident account," that is to say, the payment did not happen. This document was stopped. A bank transfer was used to transfer the money from one account to another. That is why I drew your attention to that a few moments ago, that this was transferred from one account to another and that the previous order had nothing to do with this last one. Because according to what the Prosecutor said, it would turn out that Mr. Stojic and Mr. Jelavic gave an order and that I, on the basis of that, collected money from the bank account of the civilian part, but that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. That is exactly the reason I selected this particular -- one of these -- this particular transaction as one of the ones to ask you about. What you indicate on the card is that you did in fact sign for having received the cash. Your signature is there, and we can see it on the lower left part of the card; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you see what it says down here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you receive the cash -- so are you saying you signed a receipt for cash that you didn't actually get?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the transaction was stopped straight away because it was realised that -- well, you see that all of this is happening on the 17th of April. So what was realised was that it wasn't from that account, because -- I mean, the person who was working on this banking transaction made a mistake, and that is why it was stopped. A new form was issued on the basis of which cash was withdrawn. It is not displayed here though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the new request, the new request, is it not, is the one that is followed that is signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Jelavic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a new request; a new order for payment. I don't know whether you understood the principle involved. First, there is this request for cash withdrawal; then after that an order is issued -- or, rather, this sale document, as it is called in banking, this form; and then this follows afterwards. When they got this form, when they got this request, when they did this, they see that the two did not match. They stopped this, cancelled this, issued a new form that had to correspond to the new request for cash withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be a good idea if the witness would put these documents on the ELMO so that we could all see them. Every time it's a series of documents pertaining to a single transaction that are under a single number, so it's hard to see what we're talking about. As for this, what he referred to just now, perhaps the witness could put all three on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have the third form, where you can see that I collected money from that giro account. So we have the one that was stopped and then we have the request for cash withdrawal. We haven't got the third form from which you can see that I collected the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you about this - counsel can pursue it if he likes on cross-examination - but at the end of the day, literally perhaps, on the 17th of April, 1993, you nonetheless collected 400.000.000 Croatian dinars; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you could turn next to Exhibit P 10302, sir, can you confirm that this reflects a transaction on the 30th of April, 1993, concerning the Croatian dinars, approximately 118.486.000?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can see, again, from this account, that this is again taken from a foreign currency savings account; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does that, again, reflect your sit on the one form, the receipt, what I'll call the receipt, indicating that you received that cash on the 7th -- excuse me, the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like my signature. That means that I did. Well, yeah, actually, it says here that it was me, so I guess it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the document appears -- the signature on the form appears to be consistent with all your other signatures that we've seen, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, again, can you confirm by looking -- is there anything on this document that you can tell us again whether you received the money on that day in either Croatian dinar or deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 97.600 deutschmark. If you look at the upper right-hand corner, you will see my signature. We should have a better copy. There should be a specification of the banknotes that were collected on that occasion. That should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, again, we can just confirm, as we saw one or two of these yesterday, that the typical practice then I take, as what you've informed us yesterday and today, is if the money was converted and taken out in a different form of currency, the typical indication would be that you or whoever would sign it above that box, where we can faintly see your signature; and then, usually, you would indicate the denominations in which the money was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct -- or rather, the exact banknotes in which the payment was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The one we saw at the end of the day yesterday was of the 150 1000 deutschmark notes, the ones that you said looked very nice. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Rupcic, changing topics --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. But on the last page of this same document, well, you have a review of all the monies incoming and outgoing through that account and the date when the withdrawals, cash withdrawals, were made. So you can see exactly how much money there was, and the total amount of money deposited in that account was a million marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So we can see on the 31st of December, 1992, approximately 1.000.000 -- or 1.000.000 deutschmarks were in the account, and then that money was then drawn on in the various transactions that we have that we see here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It is a banking document, and you can see the transactions on the basis of that account or savings book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Including on the 30th of April, 1993, the transaction we were just talking about is 97.600 deutschmarks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in your experience in serving for quite some time in the finance section of the HVO military, can you tell us, to your knowledge, how were the basic financial decisions of the Ministry of Defence or the HVO military, how were these determinations made and by who?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: It's what I could learn from Mr. Majic. He would receive orders from Mr. Jelavic, and he would convey part of that order to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I take it from your extensive involvement in these matters and later, in fact, you became an assistant minister yourself, you told us yesterday, so I'm going to press you about -- on this a bit. How did -- who did you understand made the decisions about how the money of the HVO military or the HVO Ministry of Defence or Department of Defence, how those monies would ultimately be spent? Who determined the budget? Who approved the expenditures?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this when we talked. I didn't talk -- take part in the conversations and wasn't present as to who decided, who made the decisions; but I did say, from what I knew from my information, because I was sitting in the same office as Mr. Majic, that Mr. Boban decided about the priorities. And as money was always lacking, Mr. Boban would set the priorities, and then would convey them to Mr. Jelavic; probably Mr. Jelavic to Mr. Majic; and then Mr. Majic down the line to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your -- you said in your interview in 2005, and you said again over the weekend, that those decisions were made by the head of the Defence Department and his senior advisors; that is, Mr. Stojic and the senior members of the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission. This is a leading question, and I don't think it should be allowed. The witness has told us what he knew. He says that he said this several times during the interview and statement. So if the Prosecutor wishes to elicit an answer like that, he should not do it in such a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I disagree, Your Honour, because I have the right to challenge the testimony of this witness. I've not endorsed this witness in everything that he says, and I have right to, absolutely the right to, challenge his testimony, as is done in all the courtrooms in this Tribunal every day, and I do not accept his testimony on this as being completely inconsistent with what his testimony is before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas. We shall try to understand how this worked in financial terms. We understood that you were working in an office together with Mr. Mazic. You were sharing the same office, and you told us that Mr. Boban was not far removed from there. So you were working very close to the decision-making bodies. When it came to paying the salaries of the soldiers, who said, "We need to go and go the money"? Who told you to go and fetch the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majic would be the person who told me to go down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As your senior, who told Mr. Majic that the soldiers needed to be paid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, from what he said -- or rather, he was called to the office of Mr. Jelavic by Mr. Jelavic, and that's where they made the arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, as far as Mr. Jelavic was concerned, was it him who took the decision or was there someone else telling him that he had to pay the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge, I can only say what I heard, not what I saw personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since you were some kind of a department, were there meetings with everyone, Majic, Jelavic, yourself, Boban, possibly others? Were there staff meetings or were you the courier? Were you the errand boy? Were you told to go and collect the money and withdraw the money? Were there meetings which you yourself attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not present. So Mr. Jelavic would hold meetings with his immediate associates, and at those meetings were Mr. Majic, Mr. Medic, Mr. Slobodan Pezer, Mr. Ignac Rakic. I did not attend those meetings, which means that I was a clerk of a lower level, a courier, as you say, and my main job was to go and bring them the money back. As to the other affairs, to decide upon salaries and everything, they would do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand rightly, in the decision-making process, you had no role whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, if you're asked questions upon Mr. Stojic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Jelavic, are you able to answer or are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer and tell you everything I know. There's no reason for me to keep anything secret, but I can't tell you about things I don't know about. I've already said, I've already told you what I know. I've already told you what Mr. Majic said, because we sat opposite each other in the office. So when he came back, he said, "Mr. Boban ordered such-and-such." Now, whether he ordered it to him directly or via Mr. Jelavic, I don't know. I don't think Mr. Boban ever addressed Mr. Majic directly. The link there was Mr. Boban, Mr. Jelavic. And, as I said yesterday, Mr. Stojic was in Mostar, and I see no way in which he could have communicated with Mr. Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to conclude this, as regards Mr. Boban, did he summon you in his office and did you talk to him, or did you actually never talk to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he never talked to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a few minutes ago, a few minutes ago, you were quite prepared to say, even though now you've said you never saw Mr. Boban make these decisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You Honour, I do apologise for interrupting my learned friend's questions and I will try not jump up too many times, but it might be the same to raise an objection as matter of law. My learned friend has said at paragraph -- line 25 of page 14 and the start of page 15, and I quote: "That I have the right to challenge the testimony of this witness." Your Honour, these proceedings start, in my respectful submission, with a premise that the Prosecution call witnesses of truth. They call witnesses in good faith that they're going to testify truthfully to Your Honour. What my learned friend seeks is to it cross-examine his own witness. This is entirely inappropriate, in my submission. Just because he's called a witness and doesn't like what the witness says does not give him the right, absent hostile animus, to cross-examine a witness, and I do object, Your Honours. He should confine himself to evidence in chief. He has chosen to call this witness. He must live with the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honour, Mr. Khan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Khan is entirely wrong on this point. When a party calls a witness, they do not endorse that witness. I don't vouch for Mr. Rupcic or any other witness. The Prosecution calls witnesses to present certain evidence to the Chamber. I don't have the luxury of choosing which witnesses may have knowledge of a particular topic. If Mr. Rupcic was in the position he was in to have this information and to sign these forms and collect this money, he is that person. He is not the person of my choosing. When a Prosecution or any party calls a witness, they are not endorsing that witness or vouching for the witness. They're simply taking the opportunity to put that information before the Chamber. Now, it happens every day, because I know as I closely follow the other trials and my colleagues and senior trial attorneys in other trials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right. Mr. Khan is right, and you are also right. The only problem is, Mr. Scott, that in this budget and financial system, we try to understand who was taking the decision. We're trying to understand what part he was playing in this. He was 27 at the time. There were other people whom you could have called to testify. I don't know if they are alive or if they are still around, like Mr. Jelavic, Mr. Majic. When your investigators realised what the problem was about and the role played by this person in the entire system, maybe you should have called somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To respond briefly to your question, of course Mr. Boban is dead, Mr. Jelavic is a fugitive from justice, Mr. Stojic is one of the accused in this case. So the people -- many of the people that are in this chain of command are certainly not available to the Prosecution. Further, further, Your Honour, it's not correct, unfortunately, to say that this witness didn't have knowledge of that, and that -- which is precisely my point. The witness has displayed on previous occasions much more extensive knowledge of these matters after his extensive involvement in these matters than he is now prepared to tell the Court, unfortunately, because he was quite clear in explaining the budget process to me, both in 2005 and two days ago. And for whatever reason, now he doesn't want to tell the Chamber what he has said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to point one thing out and to make things clearer linked to what the witness said previously and to my intervention when Mr. Scott asked his question, because he said you said this earlier on during your examination. I'd like to refer to the 21st of June, 2005, at 1405 hours of this witness's testimony. Unfortunately, I haven't found it in the transcript but I will do so before I begin my cross-examination, where the witness says, "When I went to Grude, which means Mr. Boban would either tell Mr. Jelavic or me or Mr. Majic what to do with the money, and then we would prepare the money. We would -- people would come. They would sign in order to take over the money, which means that that unit or any unit received the money, took over the money." So that's what the witness said when he was interviewed by the Prosecutor, and that is why I consider, Your Honours, that you comment is completely justified, and he said what he knew about this. Now, if the Prosecutor was not satisfied with the witnesses knowledge, he cannot now insist upon something else. But, quite simply, if this witness doesn't have the knowledge or doesn't know about it, the Prosecution had the choice. I don't know what he meant when he referred to Mr. Stojic, but people who worked on this job. People, they were accessible to the Prosecution. The Prosecution chose this witness, and he said he knew nothing further than what he's already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we're not going to waste any more time. Please proceed and put your questions to the witness. If you feel that the witness does not fully answer your questions, as you've said -- Witness, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to avoid any misunderstandings, I don't want you to misunderstand me. I did happen to meet Mr. Boban in the building, run into him, because we were in the same building. So I did bump into him, but I never communicated with him except to say, "Good morning," "Good afternoon, Mr. President," and things like that. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go back, Witness. If you could turn again please to P 10275. 10275.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me. Maybe it's been written down wrongly. I can see you're not looking at the correct document. It's the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness needs some assistance. He doesn't need to be able to find the document. 10275.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, this, again, is the chart that you drew in your own hand in 2005 and which you testified about yesterday. Now, a few moments ago, you were -- even though you've just told the Chamber that you did not have personal discussions with Mr. Boban about budget matters or the allocations or approvals of expenditures, you were quite prepared, a few most ago, to say that it was Mr. Boban who made those decisions, even though you've now said you don't have personal knowledge. You didn't see him do it. But, sir, is it your position, looking at this chart, that it was Mr. Jelavic who took on himself to make all the financial decisions for the Ministry of Defence and the HVO military? That he approved all the expenditures, how the money, how the budget of that department would be spent, that was Mr. Jelavic who did that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, the day before yesterday, I tried to explain this to you. As far as I know, in Herceg-Bosna, the system was taken over from the Republic of Croatia as it was there. The president of the state, if I can put this in the vernacular, was the be all, end all. He was the top guy. The prime minister, president of the government, Mr. Valentic, and all the others were figures, if I can put it that way. So the gentleman mentioned will forgive me for putting it this way and giving my interpretation: Mr. Boban was the number one percentage down there, and the rest were just actors in lesser roles. What I want to say is that Mr. Boban had the main say, and I mentioned this several times to you in what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, you did, sir, and you also mentioned a number of other things. Yes, of course, we know that Mr. Boban was the president of Herceg-Bosna. That is well known in this case and not disputed, but you just said the other persons had lesser roles. Yes, again, we can agree as a matter of hierarchy that they were lesser roles; nonetheless, the Minister of Defence in any government is a senior government official. Now, is it your position that Mr. Stojic had no role in the operation of the department of which he was the head?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that he didn't have -- or had no role, but is it logical to you that Mr. Boban was sitting up there with us and that Mr. Stojic was sitting over there in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question is: How did you communicate with Mr. Bandic, for example, Mr. Zeljko Bandic, when you had dealings with Mr. Bandic in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first dealings with him was when Mr. Majic said that I had to go to Opuzen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, answer my question. My time is limited. When you had dealings with your counterpart at the finance department, Mr. Zeljko Bandic, how did you communicate with Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to explain to you, my first contact. Well, we got to know each other in Opuzen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I did not ask you about your first contact. I did not ask you about your first contact. Listen to my question, please: How did you have contact with him? Did you drive to Mostar every time you spoke with him? Did you have a telephone? Did you have a fax machine? Did you have a radio? How did you communicate with Mr. Bandic, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had telephone communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see. So you rule out the possibility that Mr. Jelavic could have telephone communication with Mr. Stojic in Mostar, just like you had telephone communication with Mr. Bandic in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't exclude that, but I don't -- can't talk about something that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it's your testimony today that you have not previously indicated that it was the head of the Department of Defence and his senior assistants who made the -- the financial decisions for the Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to you loud and clear that at the top-most level is where the decisions were made. Now, you can interpret that as you see fit, but that's what I'm telling you. At the top-most level is where the decisions were made, because we did not have enough money, sufficient funds, and so we were always in debt for food, for weapons, for fuel, for the soldiers' salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which top level --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our soldiers always wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, but again our time is limited. These decisions were made, and I want to be very clear, at the top-most level. So which top-most level are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we're talking about Mr. Boban. Now, whether he conveyed them to Mr. Stojic or Jelavic directly, well, it's logical to me that he would say it to Mr. Jelavic directly; otherwise, he would have to call Mr. Stojic up in Mostar. Mr. Stojic would have to call Mr. Jelavic back in Grude, and there's no logic there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Witness, I will put the question the other way round. Admittedly, Mr. Boban, President Boban, took all the decisions. In French, it was translated like this: "He was God Almighty." As he had the highest authority, he responded to the request or applications made by his subordinates, yes or no, or did he take his decisions randomly, without anything to rely upon? If he decided after having had these requests or applications, either you, Mr. Bandic, Mr. Jelavic, or were you able to make any applications or make any requests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of requests? Could you explain what you mean there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to financial matters, of course, because we are talking about financial issues, when people put in a request, a financial request, in light of your various needs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, you see: I can speak about my own level. I and Mr. Majic keep the books regularly, with all the obligations towards the procurers and what we had to send out to the soldiers, and that report was sent on a daily basis to Mr. Jelavic. Now, who Mr. Jelavic sent it on to I don't know. All I know is that every day, at Mr. Boban's, delegations would arrive from different municipalities. Now, what they talked about, what they discussed, I really don't know. I do know that after meetings of that kind he would call Mr. Jelavic, and then after that payments arrived from Konjic, for example, the civilian authorities. After that, the HVO in Konjic would be paid out a certain amount of money, as much money as there was available; or from Zepce, for example. Mr. Jelavic would come to us and say, "Prepare such-and-such a sum for the HVO of Zepce." So there wasn't a system in place because we didn't have enough money. So you couldn't meet all the requirements which you had, all your obligations. You would have to decide on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. My last question on this topic: As far as you know, out of Mostar where Mr. Stojic was, let's say he had already put in a request, a money request. Would this have been accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did he put in his request to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if he turned to "God Almighty," I mean; the highest authority, as you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic could put in a request to Mr. Boban, and he could issue an order to Mr. Jelavic. So that's why I'm asking a request to whom. You can't table a request or you don't table a request to your subordinates. You issue orders to your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a final time on this point before moving -- hoping to move on. Is this correct, sir, is it correct, sir, that on the 20th of June, 2005, it was the head of the Defence Department and his assistants who made the decisions regarding the financial operations of the department? "Both small and large priorities were to say were in charge of high-level officials," isn't that in fact what you said in 2005 and again what you said in the previous couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only natural that everything was decided at highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At no time in that -- in these prior discussions did you indicate Mr. Boban making the decision. You said it was Mr. Stojic and the people in the Ministry of Defence who made these decisions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please speak one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few moments ago I read an excerpt of the witnesses statement where he said, I think, words are being put into his mouth and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if the Chamber would like me to read the transcript of the interview, the recording, and I want to indicate this was an audio recording. This isn't investigator's notes. This was an audio recording of what the witness said on the 20th of June, 2005. It was being discussed about these matters and the payment of payroll and financial operations and in connection with Mr. Boban the context. I'll just start, and so there's no question about it, I'm reading, I'm referring to page 30 of the transcript of his audio recording given on the 20th of June, 2005. I asked the question: "Using the example again of the earlier time period, when you were getting these approvals or authorisations from Mr. Boban, did that continue or did other persons -- did somebody else take that role?" And then Mr. Rupcic goes on to say: "The Ministry of Defence came to its full existence and operation. It was independent. With a note that it reported at the end to the government of Herceg-Bosna." "Okay. As I want to be clear," my question, "my next question is: Specifically, what became the Ministry of Defence not the broader government or Herceg-Bosna government? So I understand financial affairs that were internal to the Ministry of Defence, what was what was the structure for organisation or approval of expenditures or transactions?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RUPCIC
utterances.text: "The Minister with his assistants was making decisions regarding priorities." Then on the top of page 31, he goes on. When I asked him about setting the priorities, he says: "Both large and small priorities were in charge of high level officials." In the entire context of that discussion on those pages, and before and following, he indicates: "Those decisions are make by the head of the Defence Operation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say something to the Prosecutor. When we talked over the last few days, we came to the conclusion that the Ministry of Defence was established towards the ends of 1993, and then it wasn't Mr. Stojic who headed the Ministry of Defence. So can how can I say then that Mr. Stojic took part in decision-making at the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're playing on words. You know that it was the Defence Department before it was called the Ministry of Defence; and on your chart, the chart that you drew, which is P 10275, you put Mr. Stojic at the head of the Department of Defence. Everyone in the courtroom, at this point, knows that what was the Department of Defence later became called the Ministry of Defence, but virtually it was exactly the same organisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may make a short intervention. It appears from the gentleman's answers over the course of the last couple of days, prior to his testimony, he provided the Prosecution with certain information with respect to his particular statement taken in 2005. That information, which the gentleman is now trying to bring out to our attention, was not recorded. We have no proofing notes. We have no supplemental. I think we are at a distinct disadvantage and so is the gentleman here, and I think that - I'm not trying do defend him - certainly it would appear that he should at least be given the opportunity to explain in full what exactly he told the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor can then, if you wishes to impeach his own witness with the statement, he may try to do so. But at least, I think, the gentleman should be given a full and fair and complete opportunity to explain exactly to us what he told the Prosecutor in a private session that was not recorded, no supplemental, no proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for a moment. Of course, the Chamber can give all the time to this witness that it likes, that it desires to do so, and I am certainly not opposed doing that, because I certainly agree that we should get to the truth of this matter. I do however, before whatever the Chamber decides, want to be clear in response to something Mr. Karnavas has said. The Chamber well knows that there -- we meet with every witness in preparation for their testimony. That is not a secret. There is nothing sinister about that. It happens all the time. I expect, when the Defence witnesses come, the Defence will do exactly same thing. Now, in terms of a proofing note, what the Prosecution normally does, not only in this case but I think other cases, is where in the preparation of a witness, in meeting with a witness, some of these witnesses may have been interviewed years ago; and in reviewing the matters, if there is something in fact new or different that it comes out, then we do provide that in a note to the Defence so that they're advised of that. The key point there is if it's something new or different. What -- unfortunately, what Mr. Rupcic said on the weekend, on Saturday and Sunday, was, in fact, entirely consistent with what he said in 2005. There was no reason to prepare a proofing note on something where he was consistent with what he has said before. It is only today that he begins to give different answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, in 2005, you were interviewed by the OTP, and you answered a number of questions. This weekend you met Mr. Scott and his associates. At any point in time did you question what you had said in 2005? Because I'm sure you were reminded of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Everything I stated then -- well, with some small changes that we stated -- well, you see, I thought that the Ministry of Defence came into being in the beginning of 1993, but that was not the case. It actually happened at the end of 1993; that is to say, that I and the Prosecutor when we talked stated that on the basis of the documents that he showed to me. Now I would like the Prosecutor -- well, he read something out a few minutes ago. I would like him to say what it is that I said differently now in comparison with the statement I made then. I didn't really. I really would like the Prosecutor to say what it is that I said differently now than I did in 2005. However, it is only natural to me that Mr. Boban was at the head. It is only natural for me that he cooperated with Mr. Prlic, Mr. Tomic, Mr. Bruno Stojic, that he cooperated with them. But, again, I'm telling you that Mr. Boban was in Grude; not Mr. Stojic, not Jadranko Prlic, not Mr. Neven Tomic. They were in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, on what matters would the witness have said something different from what he said in 2005? I don't have anything to rely on; so if you have a piece of information that is very accurate, perhaps you could put the question to him. In 2005, you said such-and-such, today you are saying such-and-such; and then we can compare the two. Otherwise, it's quite impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did that a few moments ago. I referred to specific statements of the witness in 2005. I read those from the transcript of the interview. Unfortunately, Your Honour, I think, because of the limitations of time, we're going to have to move on. This is obviously substantially slowed down the progress of the Prosecution's examination, and we maybe have to -- we may require additional time to finish the examination. But under the circumstances I don't feel that I can belabour the point longer. I think we have made our point clear, Your Honour. What has been said before is different that what has been said today, although the witness then just said, a moment ago, "Well, of course, all these people were cooperating and working together," which logic would dictate was the case. If the Chamber would give me a moment to organise --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I would just like to say to my colleague and to the Court that we indeed did get the transcript of this witness, but we also got some changes in relation to the statement that we got the transcript of, on the 14th of May, 2007. I believe that the Judges have this explanation. In this explanation, dated the 14th of May, the Prosecutor is telling us now that the witness changed some of the things he said. In paragraph 5, in the last paragraph, the witness says: "The question was put to me who it was who allocated financial resources, and I answered that it was Mr. Mate Boban and Mr. Bruno Stojic. That is wrong, because I received orders only from my immediate superiors, and they were Mr. Ante Jelavic and Mr. Pero Majic. "By stating the names of the two gentlemen," okay, okay, "I made an assumption that is not based on certainly knowledge. The only persons who can speak about the possibility of Mr. Boban and Mr. Stojic in distributing financial means are Mr. Jelavic and Mr. Majic." This is what the Prosecutor wrote down decidedly in relation to this witness, and we have heard this repeated time and again now, because the witness keeps saying that he didn't know how the line functioned and that he did not receive orders from above. That is why I'm surprised to hear the Prosecutor say that the witness today is changing something in relation to the previous statements he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm beginning to understand what this is about. It seems, Witness, that in 2005, according to what the Prosecutor has told us, that you had said, as far as appropriation of funds were concerned, it was Mr. Boban and Mr. Stojic who were in charge. This was in 2005. Now it seems that you have told the Prosecutor that there was a mistake, and that it wasn't that that we needed to understand. You wished to correct this. Is this how things happened, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me respond to that, because I have the statement. In fact, the Prosecution position is that the statement exactly supports what the Prosecution has been trying to clarify these last few minutes. I'll be happy to provide a copy to the Chamber, if the Chamber doesn't have it. It is correct that the witness was briefly seen again in -- on the 14th of May, 2007. At that time, he provided -- he did make a correction, and I will simply -- and if the Chamber has the document, the chart that we've been looking at about it, I would ask the Chamber to have that at hand. This is what the witness said: "I drafted an organisational chart of the HVO Defence Department headed by Bruno Stojic. I stated that this chart reflected the situation from August 1992 to the end of 1992, beginning of 1993. However, this should be changed in 'August of 1992 to the end of 1993.' During the mentioned time frame, Mr. Stojic was not the head of the department for the whole period, because at a certain point of time, he was replaced by someone else whose name I can't remember." He goes on to say, in the next paragraph: "I drafted an diagram of the organisational chart of the HVO MOD headed by Bruno Stojic." That was a separate chart that we didn't look at because changes of the changes that were made, and the witness corrects it by saying: "This is not correct, because Bruno Stojic was never the Minister of Defence." The difference, Your Honour, being, as I said a few moments ago, we're talking about a difference of terminology, and these matters are not, I don't believe, disputed by anyone in the case. Let me finish. Let me finish before I'm interrupted. It is absolutely clear, the Chamber's heard evidence, that in August of 1993 what had been called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna declared itself to be the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and certainly terminology changes were made at that time. What had been called a "Department" became the "Ministry," and that was then reformed. Toward the end of 1993, these changes were put into place. I don't believe it's also dispute that had Mr. Stojic ceased being the head of the Defence Department in November of 1993. The witness is correct. What the witness did confirm is the chart that we've looked at the last two days, the chart which is P 10275, was an accurate chart from not just until the beginning of 1993 but from August 1992 to the end of 1993, provided that both the witness and the Prosecution agree that at the end of that period Mr. Stojic was replaced by someone else. That's what the correction is and the statement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be -- briefly respond to the closing argument made by the Prosecutor, because all of this is their spin on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may have the courtesy, please. I'm rather shocked and appalled that Mr. Scott would try to misrepresent the fact to the Trial Chamber. It is not a mere changing of terminology. Either Mr. Scott doesn't know his case or he's deliberately misleading the Bench, because you have to look at the legal instruments. You have to look at the legal instruments and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- when you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas. I will let you have the floor. But if I were to be misled, you have to be an early bird. So rest assured nobody can mislead me. So I have documents in front of me. I'm trying to understand. This is why Judges put questions, and you cannot imagine that you can mislead a Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. My point is this, Mr. President: When a department becomes a ministry, it is not just a mere change of terminology. You have to look at the legal instruments, and you have to look at those instruments to determine what the actual changes are. I think that's something that the gentleman wished to -- to explain, and perhaps that might be one of the problems. Mr. Scott is looking at it, for whatever reason, maybe he's just, you know, unaware of the difference, but he's looking at it as a mere terminological issue; whereas, the witness is looking at it from a structural point of view. Also, I think what has to be kept in mind is that the one portion that was read out by Ms. Nozica, which is the gentleman indicated that when he gave his statement he made certain assumptions, and I think that's the critical aspect of it. Perhaps if the gentleman was asked about any -- why he made those assumptions or how he could make those assumption, that may assist us in getting to the truth. But it seems to me that the Prosecution is trying to impeach his own witness, and, indeed, has gone so far as to say the witness is confabulating today, being less than honest, being economical with the truth, however you wish to put it, simply because the gentleman during the proofing session gave fuller and fairer explanations than at the time of the statement. And to quote Mr. Scott, when his witnesses impeached on matters, he routinely says, "Well, it's only understanding that witnesses may make some variations or may have some changes to their testimony." Now when he has his own witness, albeit he's a Croat and he's saying things that Mr. Scott doesn't like, all of a sudden the witness is being economical with the truth. I don't think that's very fair. If Mr. Scott wishes to impeach his own witness, I suggest that he show him the statement and give the witness an opportunity to respond, both the question and the answer of the statement, and give the witness to give a fuller and fairer explanation. And if the witness has indeed explained these matters differently during the proofing session, I think that's critical and that should -- that should be noted for the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, and then perhaps my learned friend can respond in toto to both submissions. Your Honour, I am fortified, of course, that one has to be an early bird to mislead the Trial Chamber, but misleading a witness, of course, is another matter. It's my respectful submission that procedure is there to safeguard the administration of justice; and, in my respectful submission, my learned friend innocuously, of course, has erred in his dealing with this particular witness. I do, for the record, object to my learned friend giving evidence, in effect, as to his theory of the case whilst the witness is under oath present in court. Your Honour, I have -- and Your Honours will be familiar with the jurisprudence of this court. What my learned friend should have done, if he wished to declare this witness hostile, is to establish to Your Honours' satisfaction either a hostile animus or that this witness - and this is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal - and I quote, "is not desirous of telling the truth." Your Honour, the way he should have done that is, in the absence of the witness, make submissions based upon the prior statement which my learned friend has read out and the testimony elicited at court today. But to have a mish-mash of evidence, examination-in-chief, and cross-examination, when he doesn't like it, is singularly inappropriate. My learned friend, with the greatest of respect, has caused this needless spending of time because of the procedure he has chosen to adopt with his own witness, given the statement which is taken by the Prosecution themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Scott, you may respond to that but the witness has raised his hand. What do you want to say, because you are the most concerned here? What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say one more thing. When I talked to Mr. Scott, I said to him then these little boxes, the way I drew them, stayed roughly until the ministries were formed, or rather, the government of Herceg-Bosna. However, I said that I was not sure and that I could not claim until when the people whose names are written in this these little boxes remained there. So I would like Prosecutor to say where it is I deviated from my original statement when I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's now a number of things have been said in the last ten minutes by two counsel and the witness. I'll try to respond to as many of them as I can remember at the moment. I have to start out, Your Honour, by observing that is so often is the case that Mr. Karnavas get to his feet and he makes a multitude of allegations and attacks about everything, you know, including the kitchen sink, so to speak, and attacks the good faith of the Prosecution and everything else. So it becomes very difficult to give a short response to all the attacks Mr. Karnavas has made. Now, I'm very, very aware of the procedures followed in this Tribunal and the practices, and I believe I've acted entirely consistently with those practices. Perhaps counsel didn't hear what I said a few moments ago. There was no reason to challenge or make a point of this witness's testimony, and it wasn't that the proofing session, which Mr. Karnavas would like to make sound so sinister. There was nothing different that time that would raise with the Prosecution that there was a difference of position on this. Unfortunately,, it is only today and, indeed, in some instances yesterday in which the witness has begun to give answers different than those that he gave in 2005 and different than the ones he gave and Saturday and Sunday. Now, in response to specifically to this what the witness just said, there was never a dispute and never an indication that some of the names in the boxes may have changed from time to time, and I don't think anyone in the courtroom thinks there's any dispute about that. It is clear that by November, around November of 1993, Mr. Stojic ceased being the head of the Defence Department or Ministry, whichever term one wants to use, at that time; however, that does not -- and that's what the witness said. Again, we looked at the chart. If it will make everyone feel better, when we have this, the box for Mr. Stojic up there, if everyone wants to pencil in next to it "until November 1993," we can all do that. That's not what's in dispute. To go back into some time now, the reason this dispute first started this morning was when Mr. Rupcic began giving different answers about how financial decisions were made; and, in 2005, he indicated those were made by the senior officials in the department, including the head of the department, Mr. Stojic. That's where we got -- that's where we went off the rails, so to speak, Your Honours. So let's keep exactly the issue in mind. Having said all that, Your Honour, and again because of the time limitations, I'm prepared to move on. I think the Chamber knows the Prosecution's position by this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your position is well-known. Witness, we have in front of us an organisation chart. We have small boxes here. Everybody can see these. If you were asked today to draw this organisation chart again, would you draw it in the same way or would you change things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would draw it the same way, that's for sure. However, it's only a question of whether the people whose names are written in these boxes were there. In the beginning of 1992 -- well, in 1992, these people were there. Now, Mr. Stojic and Mr. Mariofil Djidic, was there someone between the two of them, I don't know. I cannot say. It was a much higher level than the level that I was at. However, on the basis of my recollection, on the basis of people I knew, that's it. Now, how long this went on for, I don't know. How long Mr. Stojic was in that position, I have no idea. How long Mr. Prlic was in that position, I have no idea. But this is it. Now, what did I omit? I didn't draw that Mr. Boban was above all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yes. We don't see Mr. Boban's name on this organisation chart, but you are in this organisation chart; and below Mr. Jelavic, there seems to be four boxes: A traffic department, quartermaster, finance, and equipment. This organisation chart is a logistics organisation chart or a budgetary organisation chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the technical service, or rather, it is the material and technical resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of a technical nature, you mean, this organisation chart? Or is it an organisation chart which represents a decision-making network, a financial decision-making network?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are a man who has gone to university. You had a high rank. You were a general. You were in positions of responsibility, so I'm sure you understand my question. You are a learned person. So if I ask you whether this organisation chart is part of a decision-making process in budgetary terms, either you say "yes" or you say "no." In that case, you may respond that this is an organisation chart intended for logistic purposes solely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I respond, if I drew the logistics base for you, and if I mentioned to you all the different divisions, the traffic department, the quartermaster department, finances, et cetera, all of these boxes would have to be thrown out, and then you would have, say, Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Bruno Stojic, Mr. Djidic, Mr. Jelavic, Mr. Majic, and then me. As for the rest, I mean they are absolutely irrelevant, if we're only talking about finance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us imagine that the HVO needs to buy a satellite telephone. In that case, the decision to buy this satellite telephone, would that be part of the organisation chart you have drawn up here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's made within the frameworks of the chart. And within in the central logistics base, the decision is made that something has to be purchased; so then a request is tabled to have the necessary funds okayed. Mr. Jelavic asked for that. He is given the okay for the funds, and then the object is procured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our here, and we shall move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have 30 minutes left; 30 minutes, not 307.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think I would use 307, Your Honour, but I appreciate the Court's indulgence. If we're not in open session, Your Honour, we can go back into open session. Are we back into it? It appears that we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention next to the -- to Exhibit P 00102. Sir, I'm showing you this document as a basis to ask you a couple of follow-up questions. This is a decree dated the -- well, it's coming. It is dated the 14th of October, 1992. It says, however to be effective, at the end of the last page, Article 10, on 1st of October 1992, over the name and title of Dr. Jadranko Prlic, "President." I note the word "President" of the HZ HB HVO. Did you become aware in your involvement with the financial -- financial dealings of the HVO, and as of today you've said Herceg-Bosna more generally, efforts to collect such things as taxes, customs, duties, that sort of things as part of the revenues of that entity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct; that is to say, that I was aware of that, although it was not personally my duty or was it supposed to have anything to do with me. But I did know about this because if taxes and revenues are collected, that means that we would get money to be able to give soldiers their salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I simply note in passing, since we have it in front of us, in Article 8, do you see that, in fact, there's reference to a bank account being established for this purpose at the same Privredna Banka Zagreb in Opuzen that we've been talking about for the past two days? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We are going back to that yet again. There was no banking system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it had to be opened somewhere. I mean, companies from the area of Herceg-Bosna, if they worked with foreign countries, they had to carry out transactions through bank accounts. So how could that be done? They had to open those non-resident accounts at the Privredna Banka, or some other bank in Croatia, so that they could carry out payments vis-a-vis Germany, the Netherlands, or any other country from which they were importing goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you provide any information to the Chamber about how much revenue of this nature, from taxes, from customs, these sorts of revenues, this had; for instance, in this particular one where they make reference to a turnover tax? In any event, do you have any information that you can provide the Chamber about how much revenue in terms of taxes, customs, et cetera, that Herceg-Bosna was able to collect during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any accurate figures. It wasn't my job. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you say you don't have any accurate figures. Can you provide some information that may assist the Chamber as to your understanding of the status of those revenues, whether you can give an actual figure or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I cannot even give a tentative figure. As I said, it wasn't really in my line of work. It was no business of mine, so I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to cover it and just so the record is clear, would you be able to assist the Chamber with providing any information about that, that sort of revenue for the year? I asked you about 1992. Now I'm asking you the same question as to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Likewise for 1993, I did not know. I can talk about 1997 and 1998 when I was assistant Minister of Finance in the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that now, sir, in the interests of -- because of the time. Just let me ask you one other question about this, before we move on, again because I don't want the answers to my questions to depend on whether I use exactly the right word or not. Whether you know a specific figure, can you provide the Chamber with any information as to what percentage of the Herceg-Bosna budget or the available funds -- let me put it this way: In the funds available to Herceg-Bosna for the operation -- for its operation, do you have any ideas what percentage of those funds were provided by taxes or customs duties in either 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I cannot even make an assumption, believe me. Well, the money came either from donations or from taxes and customs. What the proportions involved were, I really cannot say. As for the total amount involved, Mr. Tomic could give you a better answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you ask you to look next please at Exhibit P 01410. This is a communication over the name Bruno Stojic, dated the 3rd of February, 1993. In your involvement in financial matters concerning the HVO, did you ever know about any efforts by the military or units of the military to collect taxes or revenue for the government?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You showed me this document the day before yesterday for the first time, and I told you then, as well, that I had never seen it before and that it is not clear to me in what way the army was involved in this, if I can put it that way. Quite simply, I cannot tell you. I mean, it wasn't a military affair to collect taxes and contributions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you have to -- I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to know that Herceg-Bosna was just in the making. There was not state of law. I mean, what does a state of law -- a state based on the rule of law mean? Everything was in the making. Everything was being created yet again. There was no financial police. There were no tax institutions. So it was very hard to force someone to pay taxes and contributions voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And those were exactly the reasons, sir, that I was asking before, if you could assist the Chamber in providing any information about what percentage of Herceg-Bosna's funding came from such sources as tax revenue or customs duties in 1992 or 1993, just to see if you would be able to assist the Chamber in that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you Mr. Neven Tomic knows that. He was head of the finance department, and he can tell you about that. I can talk about what had reached the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm not going to belabour it, sir. But just to make the record clear, you don't recall previously saying that there was very little income from taxes or customs in 1992, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you have to understand that there was a war going on in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- I do understand there was a war going on this that area. My question to you now is: Are you saying that you did you not previously state to the Office of the Prosecutor, both in 2005 and confirmed again recently that, in 1992, for example, there was very little revenue from such things as taxes or customs duties?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. That's why I'm telling you. There was a war going on. People weren't working. Nothing was working. Companies weren't working. There was a bit of trade. What was essential in terms of supplies? Was it fuel or food supplies? Well, on the basis of that, well, we did not manufacture anything. Everything had to be imported. So what was collected was collected. So that's where the collection problem was. It also depended on who was prepared to pay. Anyway, there wasn't a financial police. There wasn't an established system that would have made it possible to monitor things. Things were still in the making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you then to turn to Exhibit P 08118, if you have that, sir. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
