utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recognise this as a report filed by Mr. Jelavic, dated the 25th of March, 1994, but described as the annual report for 1993 of something called "ONP Sector"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And although there is a translation here, I would like you to say, in your own words, what does "ONP" mean? What was the ONP Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1993, when the Ministry of Defence was established, it consisted of sectors. One of these sectors was the sector of supplies, procurement, and production. So the former central logistics base turned into the sector for supplies, procurement, and production.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And, again, lest we have some problems with terminology, can you agree with me and can you indicate to the Chamber what was previously described -- what was now described as "ONP" was essentially the logistics operations of the HVO military prior to the formation of ministries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. The former SLOB turned into the ONP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you can just assist us with a few pieces of information about this report, we won't, again, have time to go through the entire report, by any means. If you can look at - and I apologise because the page numbers may not be the same in the English translation and the Croatian version - and as you turn into the -- beyond all the cover pages, there's the very first sheet. There's the cover letter, if you will, by Mr. Jelavic; then there's another cover page saying "Finance administration"; then there's the first page of text, and then getting to -- if you can turn then to the next page. But, in any event, throughout the document there are references to somebody called the "finance service." I don't know if you see any of those. But, in looking over your shoulder, I can see what you're looking at there, and I think several pages prior to that, if you look in the body of the text, I believe you'll see a number of references to somebody called the "finance service." And if you can just confirm to us, is that the section that you worked for? Again, perhaps there was a name change, but is the finances service what was the finance section or the unit that you worked with previously?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct; that is to say, that as time went by, as work went on, as more and more people were coming in, as a new establishment was being created, in the sector for supplies, procurement, and production, one of the directorates was the one for production --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go through the list of figures, there are several pages that then give various financial figures, and there is one category that is titled -- there's one subsection that's titled "Employee compensation expenses." It's on page 10 of the English translation. Can you find it? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so -- since we've spent considerable part of your testimony talking about the HVO payroll, and since that exact terminology doesn't seem to appear, if we go to the fourth item under "Employee Compensation Expenses," which is described here as "Payment of gross calculated revenue," can the Judges and the rest of us understand that that is essentially payroll?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, for example, we could see by this document that the HVO payroll during -- military payroll during 1993 was approximately 102.000.000.000 dinar?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the next point of clarification, in the document, and perhaps we don't need to find it exactly, but there's a reference in part of the document to something called -- it's in page 12 of the English document. There's something called T -- there is an abbreviation called TMS. Can you tell the Judges what "TMS" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technical material resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is that? Can you give us a further understanding of what actually means or what's involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons, ammunition, spare parts for vehicles. Well, everything that is something like that, technical resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I think you may have mentioned yesterday, but I want to come back to the topic of the -- the debt of the HVO at the end of the war in the Balkans. I don't know -- honestly, as I stand here, I don't recall if you mention a figure or not, but can you give us what you understood to be the outstanding debt of the HVO at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The debt was over 100.000.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that regard, if I could ask you to turn to Exhibit 10267, which I believe is going to be in the separate bundle. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Rupcic, this exhibit is actually comprised of four different documents, and if I can ask you to please -- if you go towards the back of the document, it's the last of the four documents which appears to be a report that you prepared around the 4th of June, 1998. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm again that that is your signature on the document and this is a document that you prepared around June 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The first part of the document indicates -- says: "The state of existing obligations on 4 June 1998 of the HVO is 342.000.000.000 and some kuna." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since we've been talking the last few days primarily in terms of Croatian dinars and deutschmarks --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. It is 342.000.000 kuna, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I apologise for that error. Can you tell the Judges though - we've heard about deutschmarks and Croatian dinar - what currency is the kuna?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 and 1995 - I don't know exactly what year this was - in Croatia, there was a change. The dinar was abolished and the kuna was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, this 342.000.000 kuna, does that bare relationship or is any part of that figure one part of the 100.000.000 deutschmark debt that you indicated a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It turns into about 80.000.000 deutschmark, if you do the math.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But can you -- are you confirming that the Chamber that this figure includes, essentially, the war debt of the HVO, which a few moments ago you said was approximately 100.000.000 deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Now, whether it pertains to the war debt or not, well, you paid your old obligations and there were new ones that were coming in. So we had probably paid the debt from the war, but with the money that was coming in 1996, 1997, 1998. However, the army had to be fed in 1997 and in 1998 as well. So you're resolving the old debt but you're getting a new one; that is to say, that we did not have enough money to cover our old debt and our new debt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I ask you to look, and if you go back, I think, one additional document in that stack or bundle, there is a document by Mr. Jelavic dated the 26th of June, 1998, if you can find that. It is addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you -- since we have you here and the Chamber saw this document on a previous occasion, did you participate in the preparation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we go below, there's a table. It's on page 2 of the English document, but if you can find the table to orient yourself, sir. Below the table, there is a paragraph that starts with the words "In the first half of 1998." It says: "The approved revenues for the HVO were," and you give information concerning the budget coming from the federation, and then that part of the HVO support coming from the budget of the Republic of Croatia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've indicated here that in kunas, for the six-month period, the budget coming from the federation was approximately 302.000.000 kuna, but the support coming from the budget of the Republic of Croatia in kuna, for the six-month period - and, again, I apologise. There's a translation error that can be seen in the original document - the support coming from the Republic of Croatia was 480.000.000 kuna; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, even by 1998, the HVO was receiving more than half of its financial support, not from Bosnia-Herzegovina, but from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But you have to know that there was an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina on helping the army of the federation, the HVO component. Also, the BiH army, as the other integral part of the army of the federation, received assistance from Arab countries. Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole had 800.000.000 for all. With this 800.000.000, they could not cover the army; then it was decided slowly to start rationalising the army. And in that rationalisation, I left the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one final question on both of the last two documents, both your document with your signature on it in June 1998 and then this report -- or this document which is also in June 1998: This was the time when the HVO was part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Witness, on page 69, line 2, you said that agreement had been entered into between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina with a view to helping the army of the federation. When you say this are you referring to 1998, not in 1993, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Rupcic, my question to you was: At the time both those last documents were prepared at that time, the HVO at that point was part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges why in both -- in both of these documents that the currency that was used by a component of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina it was -- why did you use kunas, the Croatian currency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was still no domestic currency, and it was sometime in 1998, I believe, maybe even 1999, that the convertible mark was introduced. Don't hold me to the exact date. I really don't know what that was, but thereabouts. And let me also tell you that the kuna/mark ratio -- or rather, the kuna mark was the official currency until 2000 when the official currency became the mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In turning to a final several questions, Mr. Rupcic, I'm afraid I have to go back to a question and answer from yesterday and ask you again if you would like to correct something. Yesterday, I asked you how often you saw either Mr. Stojic or Mr. Prlic come to meet with Mr. Boban, and I believe yesterday you said you saw them once. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think that's what I said, and I think that that's the truth, that that's how it was. I personally saw him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you say in 2005, and did you say again a couple days ago, that you thought that both Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic came there to meet with Mr. Boban at least once a month?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, but I said that I saw them once. I also said that I cannot confirm exactly how many times they met and where they met, but I think they would meet at least once a month. Now, whether it was from the 1st of the month to the 1st of the next month or whether it was twice within a calendar month and then not in the following month, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just briefly then direct your attention to Exhibit P 10284, which is in the -- I'm sorry. It is in the other bundle, sir. If you can find that, please, and if you can find, at the end, on what's the first page of the English translation, or the English document, excuse me, there is a number 1 at the bottom and then there's the first item that says "On 3 March," and then following. I am and I'm simply going to ask you. If you look at the information that's indicated there, is that information that you were aware of in March of 2001? You were aware of these events; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the Croatian text, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I apologise for that. Let me read a very short portion of it to you then. It says: "On 3 March, the HDZ, which had been ousted from power by the Alliance For Changes after the November elections, proclaimed the so-called 'Croat self-rule.' Four days later, I," being the representative, "decided to remove Mr. Jelavic, the Croat member of the BiH Presidency and HDZ president from his positions." It goes on and talks about the Hrvatska Banka, and then if I can then ask. I will have to read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But for those in the courtroom, if we can turn to item number 10 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's a reference again to these events. And among they are other things, at they end of paragraph number 10, it says: "on The 13th of March," 2001, "HDZ officials ordered disbanding of the Croat component of the Federation Army, followed on 28 March by a walkout of Croat officers and soldiers from their barracks." Were you aware of those events at the time they happened in 2001, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am grateful to my grave to you for having raised that question because I'm the only Croat that was convicted for self-government, and I held absolutely no position in there. I was a nobody there. Everybody else who was in that self-rule were not convicted of anything, and I who was nobody within that set-up was given a sentence of two years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is the answer to my question that you were aware of those events at the time of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've given you an answer. I was given two years' imprisonment for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you turn to -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, again, I must object with respect to relevance. What does this have to do with the indictment? In 2001, we have this event. How is it related to the indictment? At least the Defence should be notified so we know exactly what on earth is the Prosecution trying to do here, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, it relates to the status of this witness; and as you, Mr. President, yourself noted yesterday, when you read the criminal conviction or judgement against him, you will see the connection to these events. So, number one, it puts into context exactly what Mr. Rupcic was convicted for, which he's just made a brief reference to. Number two, Your Honour, you know this issue keeps being raised every time. It's same issue, the same response, and it goes all the way back to Dr. Miller in his report, going back to the original written submissions about accepting his report. The Chamber determined at that time to receive his evidence and to receive his report. But we keep having the same argument over and over again, no matter how many times the Chamber rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, receiving and accepting it are two different things. Now, is the Prosecution suggesting that the report has been accepted as evidence and is part of the case? Again, I need some clarification from the Trial Chamber. I'm not getting it from the Prosecution. They are now prosecuting my client for events in 2001. Nothing of this nature is in the indictment. Is this a truth commission? Is this something to do with the office of the High Representative that has occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina for all these years and trying to implement the peace agreement? What is this trial all about? I think it's high time for the Trial Chamber to get control over the -- over these events. What are we talking about? Are we going to go into 2007? At what point do we say here is the line of relevancy? We're not getting it from the Prosecution. At least the Trial Chamber should alert the Defence what we need to defend ourselves against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we have an indictment. Let's remain within the scope of the indictment. We have a document from the OHR. In paragraph 10, it reads as follows: "After the elections held in November 2000, a political party was formed, Alliance For Change. HNS was then established. The OHR felt that this was anti-constitutional or against the constitution, and this led to a number of consequences." So be it. This happened in 2000 and not in 1993. Even if a number of individuals wanted to do something in Mostar in the year 2000, what does that have to do with our indictment which stops in 1992? We are not going to be trying the accused on what happened in the year 2000, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, it keeps being said that the Prosecution hasn't stated its position on this, and that's just simply, once again, not true. Of course, when the original Defence opposition, written opposition, to receiving Dr. Miller's reports were filed, the Prosecution made a response. The Prosecution stated its position in writing at that time as to why this material was relevant. The Chamber had both the Defence objection and the Prosecution's response setting out its position before the Chamber, when the Chamber decided to in fact receive Mr. Miller's testimony. So it's not correct that it's not been addressed before. Then it was raised again when Dr. Miller was here. And at the Chamber's request, and, again, like today at the urging of the Defence, the Prosecution once again stated its position on the matter. I would incorporate the same comments that I made on that day, whatever day that was, and I'd be happy to go and find the transcript this afternoon and give it to the Chamber. We are not amending the indictment, but it is the Prosecution's position that this indeed is relevant to a number of issues. It's relevant to a number of issues in the indictment as to Herceg-Bosna, the joint criminal enterprise, the nature of what was tried to be accomplished, and the roles of various people in then and subsequently, including for example, including, for example, this witness, which then we have his conviction here in front us. There will be a number of ways at the end of the case, and I don't think we have to argue them now, as the Prosecution will argue, why this information is relevant to the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, let's just look at this document here in paragraph 10. It says: "In late March, HDZ radicals in Mostar moved to -- to oust that the city mayor, Mr. Tomic," and it goes on. Now, has the indictment been amended, and are the gentlemen here, in particular Dr. Prlic, is he included as one of these HDZ radicals which the Office of the High Representative is talking about? Is there a connection between this event or the events that are described in this OHR document and Dr. Prlic? I need some clarification. I don't want to wait until I'm reading the Prosecution's final brief to figure out what exactly they're trying to do with this. I'm entitled to an answer now. Second of all, second of all, if we're going to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution switch their microphone off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we're going to go going through these documents at this point in time, let me just make it very clear to the Trial Chamber that you will be opening up another Pandora's box wherein we'll have to be -- we will have to attack now and defend against the Office of the High Representative. I don't think that's the intended purpose because you can read report after report by the International Crisis Group attacking the incompetence of the Office of the High Representative. I was part of that incompetence when I worked for the Office of the High Representative. That's why I know. I know that we were violating the Dayton Peace Accords. In fact, Ambassador Hayes, the principle deputy high representative, admitted it in Brcko, during one of the staff meetings. The OHR violates the Dayton Peace Accords every day because they have to do whatever it is they have to do in order to put that poor country on its feet. That's not an issue, and that's why I don't want to get into why the office of the High Representative has been doing in Bosnia, which is why it's a mess today. We should stick to the indictment and the Prosecutor should be cut off. Anything beyond the indictment should not be coming. It should not be discussed. We're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. The Bench are finding it difficult to work things out here. Witness, perhaps you might enlighten us. We have before us a judgement which has to do about you. When I read this judgement, you have been charged with an offence which was related to embezzlement. You might be innocent or guilty, I don't know. Whatever the case may be you have been deemed to be guilty. I don't know the details of this case. One reads here that you were the only member of this self-rule or self-promulgated government, and you were convicted. Now, this judgement which has been handed down against you, were you convicted for your political activities, or were you convicted on an individual basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, Judge: I was nothing in that self-rule, self-government. All the leading figures in that self-government, as Mr. Miller says, violated the constitution; but in court, they were all released, from Mr. Jelavic, Mr. Prce, Dragan Curcic, and all the rest of them. So the Court's verdict was that they had done nothing against the state, no crime against the state. I, as a businessman, was convicted because I gave a donation to the Ministry of the Defenders, an official institution of the state. From a private company, I gave them a donation so that they could hand out the soldiers their salaries; and for having done that, I was convicted to a prison sentence of two years. The reason was that I was toppling or engaged in destruction of the state or the toppling the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thanks to my question, I'm discovering something totally new. A number of people were prosecuted, Jelavic and other people. Nothing came of it because all the other people were released, as you have told us, and the court concluded that there had been no violation of the constitution. Seemingly, when I listen to you, there is something else which comes to light. In other words, you were accused of embezzling funds, and you state that you had used that be money to pay the soldiers. That, at any rate, is what emerges. Now, we don't have the detailed information here. We don't have the information -- all the information on the case. I can only go by the indictment I have. I'm not interested in what happens afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Again, I don't want to repeat all the same arguments that we've made before. Just to respond to one of the last Defence statements that again has been made before and answered before. No, the indictment is not being amended. No, the accused are not charged with anything that happened in 2001. That does not change, in the Prosecution's respectful submission, that does not change the relevance of this information assisting the Chamber in ultimately determining what in fact was happening in the period 1992 on 1993, just as it is relevant for the Chamber to know what happened in 1939 with the banovina of Croatia. That precedes the date of the indictment, but it's highly relevant to indicate why this was being done and that, in the Prosecution's ultimate submissions, will be that it's all part and parcel of the continuing thread, exactly. We will argue that. Whether the Chamber ultimately accepts that or not, and whether anyone wants to take a contrary position, they can do so. But there are various reasons, and I'm just citing one of them, there are various reasons why this evidence is, in fact, relevant to the case, without it being amended and without the fact -- without any indication that the accused are charged with anything after 1994. But it is indeed highly relevant. I must -- I must say that, in terms of the conviction of this accused, I think the best record -- this is not, with all due respect to Mr. Rupcic, not his characterisation of it, and undoubtedly he has strong feelings about it. Undoubtedly, he does. But we have the judgement from the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that's the best statement of what the judgement, what the conviction is of. We have that document, which is Exhibit P 10303. Now final comment, Your Honour, in general is: I find it somewhat surprising that I am convinced that if the Prosecution called a witness that had some criminal conviction and the Defence wanted to attack the credibility of the witness, the Defence would be the first, as they have in the past, I believe, to put that -- to raise that conviction. But somehow, again, we have a situation where it's okay for the Defence to raise prior convictions of the witness, but it's not okay for the Prosecution to do so. Your Honour, as I said yesterday, I thought it was fully appropriate for the Chamber to have this information when evaluating the testimony and evidence of the witness. And if I didn't -- frankly, if I hadn't have provided it to you, then the Defence would have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think Mr. Praljak has stood up. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like as one of the accused and a Croat to know whether the Prosecutor supports the genocidal thesis of the Croatian nation, that every act from 1939 to 2001 is every right of the nation here considered to go genocide, and do you allow that to be put forward here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no doubt you've been helped by my learned friend's submissions on the issue. Of course, there is a distinction regarding the Defence cross-examining on the previous convictions of a Prosecution witness because, of course, that is cross-examination, point one; and, secondly, it goes to credit. It goes back to presumption that one does not attack the credit of one's own witness. Your Honour, the second issue, of course, is the service and utility of this judgement, I stand to be corrected, but it's my understanding that my learned friend for the Prosecution only started using this decision and included it in the bundle after the evidence of Mr. Miller and not prior to that. Your Honour, perhaps that's also a factor that Your Honours may wish to take in mind. But, Your Honour, I think perhaps all of this is moot. Of course, it's a matter for Your Honours, given what a decision has been taken by Your Honour, that you are not interested in what post dates the indictment. I would urge Your Honour, if you are so minded with the Bench, to uphold that ruling, and we can perhaps move on to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may respond to what Mr. Praljak has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to engage in a dialogue with Mr. Praljak, Your Honour. I would respond to Mr. Khan's comment by saying that I don't think that's a fair characterisation of the Chamber's ruling, as I have understood it. The Chamber has not so far, not to date, indicated it's not relevant. It has considered and confirmed, as the Prosecution has said, that the accused are not charged with anything outside the scope of the amended indictment, which I have now said about 23 times is the case. That is not the same thing. That is not to say the information is not relevant. Again, Your Honour, we're having the same arguments over and over again. I have concluded -- except for one additional short topic, I've concluded my examination of the witness, Your Honour. If I can finish with those two or three additional questions, I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might be allowed to say just one thing. I didn't wish to take part in the discussion. But when the judgement was mentioned, I think the information that the Trial Chamber has on its table is not complete, and that it is a form of manipulation, of sorts. The Prosecution published the judgement on the basis of the bargaining that went on with the Prosecution. As far as I know about case, I don't know too much, but I know something that the other persons accused who defended themselves in full legal proceedings, and they were released. The judgement found them not guilty. And the witness said that in a way. It was difficult to understand if we don't look at it all. So the fact as put forward by the Prosecution that there was a judgement, that is true. There was a judgement. But in the part of the indictment in which specifically one of the accused, and that is the witness present here, made a plea agreement with the prosecution for whatever reason, because he thought it was wiser for him not to tackle others, and if he wanted put a full stop, and we know that things like that do take place and plea agreements are made; whereas, others decided to take the bull by the horns and go into a full trial. So now there is no judgement in that. Now, if the Prosecutor bases his argument on that, then he must present the whole story and the full evidence, since we're dealing with the year 2000 and so on and so forth, because otherwise this is complete manipulation of information. We've just got the tip of the iceberg here, and we might arrive at the wrong conclusions, all of us, including the Trial Chamber. That's why you had difficulty to make a timely assessment of how far it is relevant and how far not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Now, Mr. Scott, from what I understood, you have just about concluded your examination-in-chief. You have two or three questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turning to a completely unrelated topic, but just to finish. Mr. Rupcic, during the time that you were in the HVO in 1992 and 1993, did you have any information about the HVO having any helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO did have helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how many helicopters did they have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know where those helicopters were based?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges whether those helicopters were used by the HVO to make flights, for example, into Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The helicopters were used to fly in food to Central Bosnia, while that was possible, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rupcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a 20-minute break, and I don't know who is going to start the cross-examination. To make sure there is no ambiguity, any more, I'd like to get back to Rule 70. Mr. Scott, do you intend to file a new written submission which would enable the Defence to file its submissions, or do you leave it at that and stand by what you said orally as regards Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we've made our position clear. I heard the Defence today say that they wanted to not be burdened by additional written submissions, and I have to say the Prosecution, to be honest, feels the same way. I think the Prosecution's made our position very clear. I think the statement of facts that have been put forth by the state of -- I think we're still in -- we can go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the witness should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's first ask the witness to leave the courtroom and then let's move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is going to start off the cross-examination? Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Pusic's Defence has no questions for this witness. We give our 30 minutes to the Defence of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours again. Good morning everyone in and around the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My name is Michael Karnavas and with me is Suzana Tomanovic. Together, we represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Let me, first, begin by asking you some questions with respect to your background. I want to make sure I have it correctly. As I understand it, you are -- you went to university and you got a degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Part of your work experience dealt with you being an inspector when you were with the Ministry of Interior, I believe. This is prior to the commencement of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In that capacity as an inspector, you were able to put to use your background in economics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say that you know a little bit about how the banking system works?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The payment bureau, the SDK, how that worked?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we will he a talk a little bit more about that. As I understand it, prior to your involvement with the HVO, you were living in Vares; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's where you're from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if you're aware, but it's part of the Prosecution's theory, that at some point the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which they claim was a criminal enterprise, was engaged in, among other things, ethnically cleansing Croats from various places in Central Bosnia. With that in mind, in Vares, could you please tell us whether, to your understanding, being from there, whether you were being ethnically cleansed by the Croats themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct; that is to say, I personally left before the conflict with the Bosniak side, or rather, the BiH army. However, the Croats from Vares were expelled by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, say, October, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe that at some point, when you gave your statement, you briefly touched upon the events in Vares and your experiences there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When I'm referring to the statement, Your Honours, I'm referring to the statement that the gentleman gave on the -- on 20th -- between the 20th and the 22nd of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, when you spoke with the Prosecutor, you also talked a little bit about the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I knew about the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You weren't part of the -- you weren't one of the founding members, but you obviously knew something of the formation and the intent behind the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not among the founders, unfortunately. I'm sorry about that. It's not that I was somebody important, but I did know why it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you share that, that reasoning, with the Prosecution when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecutor didn't even ask me that, why Herceg-Bosna had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, would you like to share that with us before I move on to my next set of questions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, what I know I will say. I will share. Herceg-Bosna was established in order to protect the Croat people that had been threatened, that had been attacked. For them to defend themselves, some - I don't know how to put this - a community called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, at some point you -- you moved to Grude and you began working with or for the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, for all intents and purposes, you've described yourself as primarily being a courier.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the basic part of the work I did; that is to say, these transactions with the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I want to make sure we understand exactly what you were now, and what you did not do during the relevant period that we're discussing here and that we're interested in. As I understand it, you were not a member of the executive authority, the HVO executive authority, the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You did not participate in any of the meetings that were being held by the executive authority when they would meet?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were not involved in any budgetary matters concerning, you know, that the civilian part, the executive authority, would be involved in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were not either subordinated to or a confidante to Mr. Tomic, who I understand was the head of the department of finance at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; that is to say, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, based on that answer, can I conclude that you did not sit down with him or he sit down with you to discuss the budgetary issues, either formally or informally, with respect to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are confining ourselves to this period, 1992, 1993, no; 1997, 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with 1992, 1993. We'll deal with 1997, 1998 later on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you didn't have an opportunity to discuss these matters with Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to giving your statement, which was over a period of three days, did you by any chance review any of the decisions in establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I was in prison, that was not accessible to me, and I didn't know what I would be discussing with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, they didn't give you advance notice of the sort of topics that they might be interested in so you could at least make some attempt to prepare yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the paper, it only said: "Talks, Mr. Prlic et al."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, during your interview, were you given an opportunity to look at any of the decisions before answering any questions concerning how the -- the Croatian Community was structured? I'm speaking about the civilian -- the HVO civilian, the executive authority.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. None of that was put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so the diagram that you prepared, which has been shared with us, and the chart, which is Prosecution document P 10275, that was on the basis of your understanding, not on the basis of you having read, analysed the decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, meaning on the basis of what was in my head at the time and what I was thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, with respect to Mr. Boban and others, you were asked several questions here today. I just want to get that out of the way since we're talking about background right now. I take it, if I understand you correctly, you did not sit down with President Boban and have any conversations with respect to issues, such as the budget or any other issue for that matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. I wrote what my position was roughly. How would I be sitting with the president? I was just an ordinary desk officer in a particular service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't call you into his office to participate or to listen in on any meetings or telephone conversations he was having?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so, earlier, when you were being questioned by the Prosecution, with respect to your diagram and with respect to what you had said earlier, would it be fair to say that your answers were essentially, other than knowing perhaps hierarchically who was your superior, as far as who was making requests and who was issuing orders, you were not in position to either have knowledge of or to be a participant of that process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not participate in that process. As for knowledge, it is what I heard from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And since you were questioned about your statement, and we have it as an exhibit as 1D 01775 - we may not need to look at it in any great detail - I just want to read something that is stated on page 9, and this would be found on 4B. This is a 28234B because we have it in different sections, your statement. You indicate that President Boban was the Supreme Commander of HVO, and he was the president of the political party. So if he said that this was to be deposited there, then it was deposited there. And if you take a look at the last part - and that's where you're cut off by Mr. Scott - the conversation goes on in a somewhat slightly different direction. Do you stand by this statement that he was the Supreme Commander and also the head, the president of the political party, and also that essentially what you're trying to say here in between the lines and what you told us explicitly today, that Mr. Boban was the number one person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As far as I see things, it was not that somebody was reinventing hot water. This was just copied from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we look at some documents, just very briefly, because of your experience prior to the conflict and then during the conflict, before the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, obviously the Bosnia and Herzegovina, within the former Yugoslavia, had a central bank, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was there also a central bank at the national level, that is, for the entire country?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What country?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. There was the National Bank of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And then every republic, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, had its own central bank.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And also as I understand it, something that is not commonly used or at least not that I'm aware of, in some countries there was a payment bureau?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Communist set-up. It was called the public accounting service, and it was used for internal payment system; that is to say, it had to do with payments made within the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In one sentence can you give us an idea of how it worked, or a couple of sentences? If you have to explain it to someone like me, how would you explain the system and the process?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say you have a company, Soko Mostar. It has an account that it opened with the SDK. They bring a money order. Say, they are paying for aluminium from their often account, and then aluminium is in Mostar, too. Now, this is a type of bank. However, the bank was used for external payments, foreign payments to foreign countries; whereas, the SDK was used for internal payments within the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So, rather than paying by cash, it would be sort of paper transactions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with the coming of the conflict, is it not a fact that at some point the central bank for Bosnia-Herzegovina collapsed or stopped to exist as it had previously existed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, it wasn't functioning as it should have been; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not function at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Can we also say that during that period of time the banks system within Bosnia and Herzegovina was also non-existent? You told us that -- you told that to the Prosecutor, and I believe you said that today as well.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that because there was not a single bank there, and there was not a central bank there. So there were no commercial banks and also there was no central bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say that there were no central bank and no commercial banks, are we just talking about the area where the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is located, or are we talking about throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this pertains to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the war, in Sarajevo they tried to establish some central bank, but you have to know what all the functions of a central bank are, from the monetary system onwards. So, basically, Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have its own money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we talked a little bit -- or you talked a little bit about the Croatian bank of Mostar. There was some references to that in your testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go through a series of documents very quickly. We're going to start off with 1D 01770.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could provide the gentleman with the documents, it might be good to assist him at this point. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, 1770, this is a request for permission for carrying out payment transfers and loan guarantee dealing with foreign entities. The date of it, you will see, is 13 October 1992. Do you see it? Have you found the document, sir? 1770.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we just look at the very first paragraph, or let's look at the second page and look at the signature line, the signature line is from a Jozo Martinovic. Do you know this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him, yes. In fact, well, actually I've heard of him. He was the Minister of Finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it says in the first paragraph that: "We are writing to you with respect to -- in respect that you consider our application for permission to carry out payment transfers and loan-guarantee dealings with foreign entities, and make an affirmative decision." This request is being made to the national bank of BiH, and it says here: "Attention Governor Stipo Andrijic." Do you know Stipo Andrijic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my professor at university.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was he not the governor of the then existing national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed to that post, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the second paragraph, it just makes an illusion to a feasibility study. I want to point that out to the Court's attention: "The founders of the bank through the adoption of the feasibility study, statute, and the contract on the founding of the bank..." and then it goes on. I just wanted to point that to everyone's attention out, because if we look at document 1D 01769, this is dated November 1992. We see that this is feasibility study on economic justifiability of the founding of Hrvatska Banka, joint stock company?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, I think, if you look at your very last page and look at the signature line of this document and the signature of the previous document, would it be fair to say that, at least to the naked eye, they appear to be the same signature, and that is from a one Mr. Jozo Martinovic? Just look at the very last page of the document, sir, and compare 1007 and 1769.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go to the next --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, 1D 01765, this is of November 10, 1992. We see that this is a decision. Have you found it, sir? You see that it's a decision. We also see at the very bottom that it's written in or signed by a Dr. Stipo Andrijic, governor of the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you aware of this document, this decision, by the way, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it says here that the decision is: "1. Permission is granted to establish the mixed ownership bank, Hrvatska Banka, Ltd. Mostar," and, "2. This decision is final." Now, if we look at the next document, to round off this series of questions, 1D 01764, again, it is dated November 10, 1992. It is again a decision, again by Dr. Stipo Andrijic, governor of the national bank Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here we see, under number 1, after decision, "the mixed ownership bank, Hrvatska Banka Ltd. Mostar, is hereby granted authorisation to conduct international money transfer and credit-warranty activities." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now were you aware of this particular decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But it would be fair to say, based on your education and background, that this would be an official document by the governor of the national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, authorising the establishment of a mixed-ownership bank, Hrvatska Banka, with the authorisation to conduct international money transfers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, we're going to move on to another subject, just very quickly to cover this. It's a small one. This dealing with the SDK or the payment bureau system. Am I to understand, sir, that the payment bureau system also ceased to exist or to function country-wide, that is, within Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a result of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All links were severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which made it then impossible or difficult for the SDK to function?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It would be fair to say, because I wasn't there in country at the time, but as I understand it, at some point there was some sort of a -- Bosnia and Herzegovina was, as well as the other republics, were transforming their economies and their economic sectors from a sort of command economy to a market economy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That hadn't occurred at this period of time. Some steps had been taken to liberalise. But for all intents and purposes, the financial structures of the country were still heavily involved or relying on the then existing system.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite natural, because they were owned by state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Okay. Now, I just want to look at two very quick documents. One is 1D 00036, so it would be 36 or 1D 00036. This is a degree. It's dated September 1992. If we look at the bottom, it says: "President of HVO HZ HB, Dr. Jadranko Prlic." We see that on 22nd September, 1992, at that session, a decree was passed on the regulation of payment transactions. 36, That would be at the front, the very beginning, properly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that: "There is decree on the regulation of payment transactions in Croatian dinars on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the immediate threat of war or state of war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go to Article 2, it talks about "Organisation units of the Social Accounting Service (hereinafter SDK), in HZ HB, shall open a subgroup of accounts within the main group of accounts, with numerical destination." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we go to Article 3, we see that: "Payment transactions in HRD..." What does HRD stand for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "... shall be registered in the subgroups of the giro accounts; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's me just stop here for a second. At that point in time was there a currency, a viable currency circulating within Bosnia and Herzegovina, given that you've already told us that at that time the central bank, for all intents and purposes, was not operating?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A currency didn't exist. Well, when the war began, in Sarajevo they printed some bonds that could be used only on the territory of Sarajevo as a sort of legal tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I want to go back to another document, and this was shown to you yesterday by the Prosecutor, I believe. It's P 00606. It's in the Prosecution binder. It's in the other binder, sir. You can -- here, for ease, because we're trying to be as efficient as we can, if you could look at that. You recall that you were shown this document yesterday, and I just want to point to -- point something out that perhaps wasn't clear to everybody yesterday. We see this is 20 October 1992. If we look at number 4, which actually should be number 3, but it's been typed in as number 4: "Budget of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," under (a), we see the terms "BHD." Now, that stands for Bosnia and Herzegovina dinar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The numbers, what do they refer to? You know, "11800-630-128." What does that refer to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be the account of the budget for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The giro account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you have one account for Bosnia -- for Bosnia and Herzegovina dinar; and under (b), the HRD, that would be the account for the Croatian dinar; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, at least from this particular document, we're able to glean, as of 20 October 1992, we have two accounts: One for the Bosnian dinar and one for the Croatian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That's it for that. I want to talk about another subject here. You're going to have to help me out here, because I'm really not an economist; and while I think I understand some of these things, the content is rather elusive. Yesterday, you talked a little bit about non-residential accounts, and, in fact, you tried to explain it to the Prosecutor when you met with him over that period of three days. But, again, if you could help me out here, first of all, please explain to us why it was essential or necessary to have a non-residential account? But maybe before you even answer that question, what is a non-residential account? So we understand. So we can start off with a proper definition of it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I can give you the proper definition, I don't know, but the substance is in this: A legal subject from one country can only have a non-residence account in other country; not a real account, a non-residential account, so not a basic account. It's a sort of an auxiliary account in a third state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Why was it necessary, then, for some folks to have a non-residential account? I mean, if they're residents of one country, why would you necessarily need a non-residential account?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the banks system wasn't functioning in the BH, which means you couldn't pay anything out of BH abroad. There was the social accounting service, which was for internal payments, but there was no bank via which you could pay into an account in Germany, Holland, Italy, or wherever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So just to make sure that I understand, you mean to tell me that during that period of time the government in Sarajevo, the government that represented the entire country of Bosnia and Herzegovina, assuming that's what it was doing, made no provisions, and it was necessary to open up non-residential accounts? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm telling you. There was not a single bank in Bosnia-Herzegovina via which you could pay in money and have that money reach Germany, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- until the Hrvatska Banka Ltd. Mostar appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, of course, we saw that that was created legally, given that there was a request, there was a feasibility study, and we have the governor of the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina authorising it legally to be established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could look at some documents relating to this, these issues that we've been discussing, 1d 001768. 1768, if you could look in your binder -- I'm sorry, it's 01768. So just look at 1768, and they're in order. They should be in order, the numbers, so you should be able to find them rather quickly. And while you're looking at it, while you're trying to find it, for the record, this is a payment agreement. It's dated 17 February 1992, and it's a payment agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. First question I guess I need to ask is: When we say it's the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at this point in time, to your recollection, 17 February 1992, had Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independent?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is February 17 now, because look at the name: Socialist Republic. All right. If you don't know, that's fine; or if you think so, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Republic. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll look --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll look at another document that will help us out a little bit. Now just looking very briefly, under Article 1, it says: "All payments between the Republic of Croatia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be carried out as of January 1992," and it goes on, "... in the domestic currency of the Republic of Croatia and the domestic currency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then under Article 2, it says: "Signatories to the agreement have agreed that they will enable their," it's illegible there, "to open non-resident accounts with the commercial banks or with the Social Accounting Service in the domestic currencies in their respective republics." And if we flip to the next page, because we don't want to dwell on this document too long, we see that it's signed. We see that it's for the Socialist Republic of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Finance Minister Momcilo Pejic. Did you know this gentleman and did he hold that position, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from this agreement, it would appear that, at least between the two countries, or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which to my understanding is sort of between the former Yugoslavia and establishing its independence, and the Republic of Croatia, we have a formal agreement that would allow then for the opening up of non-resident accounts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of this decision by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment to make. The Minister Martinovic, who signed this document, signs in the name of the government of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. That's what's written here, government of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. Mr. Martinovic was the Minister of the government of the Republic of Croatia, then he was replaced; and after that, in 1994, he was appointed as Minister of Finance of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one correction, Mr. President. I'm told that, at least in the original version, there's nothing about the Socialist Republic of Croatia, if that's what His Honour was looking at, the "Socialist" part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go on to another document, 1D 01766, this is just for comparative purposes. 1766. Here we have a decision. If we look at the bottom, it's signed by the president of the government of the RBiH, that would be the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jure Pelivan. Of course, here we have the date. It's May 8, 1992. I point to the date and to the previous date which was February, because we could see that at least there's a change in the name of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Socialist Republic to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you see that, sir? Do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 1st of March is celebrated as BH day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at this decision, here we have -- it's a decision on regulating the payments between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republic of Serbia. Just to save time, if you look at Article III, Roman numeral III, it says here: "Legal persons from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may use the claims on non-resident accounts in the Republic of Serbia for the payment of goods and services, other payments, and for the transfer of means from non-resident accounts to other persons, all in harmony with the relations in force in respective Republic." So am I to understand, sir, perhaps you can help us out here, I know you're not a jurist, you're not a trained lawyer but you are a economist, that what I'm reading here there were actual agreements, and here there is a decision allowing, permitting lawfully for persons to open up non-resident accounts, and here we have it. This one is for the Republic of Serbia. The previous one was for the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the use, in other words, the use - just to make sure I got it absolutely right and correct me if I'm wrong - the use of non-resident accounts, in either the Republic of Croatia or even the Republic of Serbia, particularly in light of what you told us that the banking system was non-existent in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the central bank was not functioning, there was nothing illegal or nefarious about that. In other words, the opening up and the usage of a non-resident account is not part and parcel or the first step or part of the step of establishing some sort of a criminal enterprise, as perhaps some may see that as?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The documents themselves show that this was legal and lawful, but exclusively because in Bosnia-Herzegovina a banking system had not been developed. From the moment a Croatian bank, the Hrvatska Banka, was established in Herceg-Bosna, I'm talking about now, from that point in time, conditions were ripe to cancel all the non-residential accounts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to adjourned now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- close all accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is another hearing in this courtroom very soon. So, sir, you will come back tomorrow to this same courtroom and we will resume our hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
